description: Planet X × SPHEREx is a public web tool that blinks NASA SPHEREx infrared images so objects that move or change stand out. A transparent pipeline aligns images to Gaia, subtracts visits, links movers and identifies known objects via JPL, Gaia and SIMBAD, scoring each candidate 0–1. It measured all five official targets (WISE 0855 via season stacking), found asteroid 865 Zubaida blindly and builds spectra on the fly. Unexplained detections are flagged for human review.
summary:
We developed Planet X × SPHEREx, a public web tool that shows the same patch of sky at different times so anyone can see what moves or changes. Users enter RA/Dec or an object name, and the tool blinks, compares and subtracts real NASA SPHEREx images, overlays Gaia stars and contamination flags, and builds 0.75–5 µm spectra on the fly from the same exposures.

A transparent pipeline aligns every image to Gaia DR3, removes cosmic rays, subtracts visits, links moving objects and identifies known ones through JPL, Gaia and SIMBAD. Every remaining candidate gets an explainable 0–1 confidence score. The tool measured all five official test targets against their catalogs, including the coldest known brown dwarf, WISE 0855, which appears only when each season's images are stacked. It also found asteroid 865 Zubaida blindly and produced zero false movers in 384 injection tests.

This matters because SPHEREx maps the entire sky every six months, but its data are hard to explore outside research teams. Our tool lets students, educators and citizen scientists explore it in seconds, while staying honest: anything unexplained is a candidate for human review, never a claimed discovery.
details:
What it does
Planet X × SPHEREx is a public web tool that shows the same patch of sky at different times, so objects that move (asteroids, nearby stars, brown dwarfs) or change (variable stars) become easy to see. Users enter RA/Dec, in degrees or sexagesimal, or an object name. The tool then blinks, compares and subtracts real NASA SPHEREx images of that spot. Every detection is labeled Known (matched in a catalog), Unidentified (a candidate for human review) or Changed, and gets an explainable 0–1 confidence score.

How it works
A classical, fully transparent pipeline:
1. Find every SPHEREx exposure of the position through NASA/IPAC IRSA and download only the cutout needed.
2. Mask hardware-flagged pixels, but never the "outlier" flag, which is exactly what a moving object triggers.
3. Align every image to Gaia DR3 and reproject all of them onto one north-up grid.
4. Median-stack each visit's exposures to remove cosmic rays.
5. Subtract each visit from the median of the others and detect sources above 5σ.
6. Reject star residuals, saturated-star zones and cosmic rays.
7. Link survivors into straight-line tracks (fast movers, hours) or measure proper motions from native-pixel centroids (slow movers, months).
8. Identify known objects with JPL sb_ident, Gaia DR3 and SIMBAD, and score every candidate on five explainable terms.
For very faint targets, the tool stacks all exposures of an observing season to go deeper.

Results
- Barnard's Star: 10.28 ± 0.77″/yr (Gaia: 10.39)
- Epsilon Indi B: 4.49 ± 0.14″/yr (SIMBAD: 4.68)
- WISE 0855, the coldest known brown dwarf, detected only in season stacks: 7.5 ± 1.4″/yr (SIMBAD: 8.15)
- RW Aurigae and R Draconis: correctly not moving
- Asteroid 865 Zubaida, found blindly: 45.7″/h (JPL: 45.8)
- Spectrum on the fly: Epsilon Indi B from 0.77 to 4.88 µm, built from 59 exposures, showing methane absorption and matching 2MASS within 7%
- Validation: 384 synthetic movers injected into real images, 50% recovered at AB ≈ 17.2, zero false movers

Benefits and intended impact
SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months, but its data are hard to explore outside research teams. Our tool lets students, educators and citizen scientists explore a brand-new NASA survey in about 30 seconds. The confidence score helps them decide which candidates deserve follow-up telescope time. A URL with coordinates opens the tool on any patch of sky, and the tool can be embedded in any web page for outreach. New SPHEREx data releases are picked up automatically.

Tools and technologies
- Language: Python
- Science: NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, reproject, photutils
- Interface: Streamlit, Plotly, HTML/SVG/JavaScript for the blink player, Aladin Lite (CDS) for sky context
- Data: SPHEREx Quick Release images (NASA/IPAC IRSA TAP and IBE), ESA Gaia DR3, JPL Small-Body Identification API, SIMBAD (CDS Sesame), 2MASS
- Testing: pytest with a headless test of every app view, plus an automated validation suite
- No special hardware: it runs on a regular laptop, fully offline for the demo

Creativity
- SPHEREx's linear variable filter makes every exposure a different wavelength, which normally causes fake "changes". We turned that problem into a feature: the same images produce a spectrum on the fly.
- A wavelength ruler under the blink player shows which slice of the 0.75–5 µm range each frame saw, explaining to users why stars change brightness between frames.
- Season stacking reveals objects invisible in any single image, such as WISE 0855.
- Two time scales in one tool: hour-scale linking for asteroids and year-scale astrometry for nearby stars.

Factors we considered
- Scientific honesty: Planet X is our motivation, not our claim. A Planet Nine–type object is about 100× fainter than SPHEREx can show, so anything unexplained is labeled a candidate for human review, never a discovery.
- Validation before trust: every result is compared with a catalog, and the method was tested with synthetic injections and null fields with no movers. Limitations are documented: saturated stars cannot be measured for brightness changes, and very slow movers cancel out in difference images.
- Explainability: no black box. Any future machine-learning filter must beat our baseline on the same injection test.
- Accessibility: keyboard control, no autoplay when the system asks to reduce motion, measured color contrast, and color never used as the only signal.
- Reliability: the demo runs offline with pre-downloaded data and cached catalog answers.
